title: IP Datagram Reassembly Algorithms
summary: Describes an alternative approach to IP datagram reassembly that keeps bookkeeping to a minimum and needs only one buffer the size of the final datagram. It can reassemble a datagram from fragments arriving in any order, with any pattern of overlap and duplication.

plainLanguage.summary: When a message is too large for the network, it is split into pieces called fragments, and the receiving computer has to put them back together. This memo gives a way to do that with a single buffer and a short list of the gaps that are still missing.

questions: what is a hole descriptor in ip reassembly
how to reassemble ip fragments in any order
what identifies an ip reassembly buffer
subtitle: A one-buffer method for rebuilding a fragmented IP datagram, whatever order the pieces arrive in.

tldr.problem: A datagram split into fragments must be rebuilt at the destination, and the fragments may arrive in any order, overlap each other or arrive twice.
tldr.mechanism: Keep one buffer the size of the finished datagram and a list of holes, the byte ranges still missing. Each arriving fragment is compared with every hole in four tests, and holes are trimmed, split or deleted.
tldr.outcome: When the hole list is empty the datagram is complete. The RFC reports a test implementation in BCPL of under one and one-half pages of listing.

facts.label: Buffer match fields
facts.value: Foreign and local address, protocol ID, identification field

today: RFC 815 is listed with an Unknown status, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. It is an explanatory memo that offers one way to implement the reassembly mechanism defined by IP, not a protocol specification of its own.

sections.title: Introduction and the Reassembly Problem
sections.content:
One of the mechanisms of IP is fragmentation and reassembly. Under certain circumstances, a datagram originally transmitted as a single unit arrives at its final destination broken into several fragments. The IP layer at the receiving host must accumulate these fragments until enough have arrived to reconstitute the original datagram.

The IP specification gives a complete description of the reassembly mechanism and one possible algorithm for it, based on keeping track of arriving fragments in a vector of bits. RFC 815 describes an alternate approach that reduces the bookkeeping, requires for storage only one buffer equal in size to the final datagram being reassembled, and can handle any number of fragments arriving in any order with any possible pattern of overlap and duplication.

A first look suggests the job is complicated: a new fragment may precisely fill the space between two fragments, may overlap with them, may completely duplicate them, or may sit in the middle of a gap without touching either end of it. The memo argues that the process is in fact extremely simple when it is expressed properly.
sections.plainLanguage: When a message is too big for the network, it is split into pieces called fragments, and the receiver has to put them back together. This memo gives a way to do that with one buffer and a short list of the gaps that are still missing.

sections.title: Holes and Hole Descriptors
sections.content:
A partially reassembled datagram consists of certain sequences of octets that have already arrived and certain areas still to come. The memo calls these missing areas holes. Each hole is characterised by two numbers, hole.first, the number of the first octet in the hole, and hole.last, the number of the last octet in the hole. This pair of numbers is the hole descriptor, and all the hole descriptors for one datagram are gathered together in the hole descriptor list.

The general form of the algorithm is simple. When a new fragment arrives it may fill in one or more of the existing holes, so each entry in the hole descriptor list is examined to see whether that hole is eliminated by the incoming fragment, and if it is, the entry is deleted from the list. Eventually a fragment arrives that eliminates every entry, and at that point the datagram has been completely reassembled and can be passed to higher protocol levels for further processing.
sections.plainLanguage: A hole is a range of byte positions in the message that has not arrived yet. The receiver keeps a list of holes, and each time a fragment arrives it works out which gaps it fills and updates the list.

sections.title: The Eight-Step Fragment Processing Algorithm
sections.content:
An arriving fragment can fill a hole in several ways: it can completely fill the hole, it can leave space at the beginning or the end of it, or it can lie in the middle and break the hole in two. If properly expressed, the algorithm compares each hole to the arriving fragment in only four tests.

The algorithm starts when the earliest fragment of the datagram arrives. The receiver creates an empty data buffer and puts one entry in the hole descriptor list, the entry that describes the datagram as completely missing: hole.first equals zero and hole.last equals infinity, which is presumably implemented as a very large integer, greater than 576, of the implementor's choice. The arriving fragment is described by fragment.first, its first octet, and fragment.last, its last octet.

The eight steps then repeat for each fragment. Step one selects the next hole descriptor, and there is nothing more to do if there are no entries left. Step two skips the hole when fragment.first is greater than hole.last, and step three skips it when fragment.last is less than hole.first; in both cases the fragment does not overlap the hole in any way. Step four deletes the current descriptor, because the fragment interacts with this hole and the old descriptor is no longer valid. Step five creates a new descriptor when fragment.first is greater than hole.first, covering the part still missing at the front of the hole, from hole.first to fragment.first minus one. Step six creates another new descriptor when fragment.last is less than hole.last and the more fragments flag is true, covering the part still missing at the back, from fragment.last plus one to hole.last. The more fragments flag matters because the descriptor that reaches from the end of the buffer to infinity can only be discarded once the last fragment of the datagram has arrived. Step seven returns to step one, and step eight says that when the list is empty the datagram is complete and is passed to the higher level protocol processor.
sections.plainLanguage: Each arriving fragment is compared with every gap in the list. If the two do not overlap, the gap is left alone; if they do, the old gap is removed and any smaller gap left at either end is added back to the list.

sections.title: Storing the Descriptors in the Buffer
sections.content:
The main complexity in the eight-step algorithm is not performing the arithmetical tests, but in adding and deleting entries from the hole descriptor list. One could imagine an implementation in which the storage management package is many times more complicated than the rest of the algorithm, since no upper limit is specified on the number of hole descriptors that will exist for a datagram during reassembly. The memo's answer is to put each hole descriptor in the first octets of the hole itself. By the definition of the reassembly algorithm the minimum size of a hole is eight octets. Storing hole.first and hole.last will presumably require two octets each, and an additional two octets will be required to thread the entries together on the list, which leaves at least two more octets to deal with implementation idiosyncrasies.

There is one obvious pitfall in this storage strategy. The eight-step algorithm must be executed before the data from the fragment is copied into the reassembly buffer, because copying first might smash one or more hole descriptors. Once the algorithm has run, any hole descriptors that are about to be smashed have already been rendered obsolete.

Scattering the descriptors through the buffer means they must be threaded onto a list, which implies a pointer to the head of the list. In many cases that pointer can be stored in a descriptor block that the implementation associates with each reassembly buffer. If no such storage is available, the memo offers a dirty but effective trick: store the head of the list in a part of the internet header in the reassembly buffer that is no longer needed, an obvious location being the checksum field. When the final fragment of the datagram arrives, the packet length field in the internet header should be filled in.
sections.plainLanguage: The list of gaps is stored inside the gaps themselves, so no separate bookkeeping area is needed. The algorithm has to run before the fragment's bytes are copied into the buffer, or the stored list would be overwritten.

sections.title: Options and the Unknown Header Length
sections.content:
The preceding description made one unacceptable simplification: it assumed that there were no internet options associated with the datagram being reassembled. The difficulty is that until the first fragment of the datagram is received, nobody can tell how big the internet header will be, because certain options are copied identically into every fragment while others, such as record route, are put in the first fragment only. The first fragment is the one containing octet zero of the original datagram.

Until the size of the internet header is known, the receiver does not know where to copy the data from each fragment into the reassembly buffer. If the earliest fragment to arrive happens to be the first fragment, there is no problem. Otherwise there are two solutions. The receiver can leave space in the reassembly buffer for the maximum possible internet header, which is not very large at 64 octets, or it can gamble that the first fragment will contain no options and, when the first fragment finally arrives, shift the data in the buffer a sufficient distance to make room. The only peril in copying the data is that the pointers that thread the hole descriptors together will be trashed, and the memo notes that it is easy to see how to untrash them.

The source and record route options have the interesting feature that, since different fragments can follow different paths, they may arrive with different return routes recorded in different fragments. That is more information than the receiving Internet module needs, and the specified procedure is to take the return route recorded in the first fragment and ignore the other versions.
sections.plainLanguage: Some IP headers carry extra options, and their size is only known once the first fragment arrives. The receiver either reserves room for the largest possible header or moves the data along when the real header size is known.

sections.title: The Complete Algorithm
sections.content:
Two further parts complete the reassembly process. First, when a fragment arrives, the receiver has to find the reassembly buffer associated with it, which requires some mechanism for searching all the existing buffers. The correct reassembly buffer is identified by equality of four fields: the foreign and local internet address, the protocol ID, and the identification field.

Second, a timer based mechanism decrements the time to live field of each partially reassembled datagram, so that incomplete datagrams which have outlived their usefulness can be detected and deleted. One way is to create a demon that comes alive once a second and decrements the field in each datagram by one. The other is to read the clock when each first fragment arrives and queue a timer call, using whatever system mechanism is appropriate, to reap the datagram when its time has come.

An implementation of the complete algorithm, comprising all of these parts, was constructed in BCPL as a test. It took less than one and one-half pages of listing and generated approximately 400 nova machine instructions. The portion actually involved with the management of hole descriptors is about 20 lines of code. The version described here is a simplification of the author's original version, thanks to an insightful observation by Elizabeth Martin at MIT.
sections.plainLanguage: To finish, the receiver matches each fragment to the right buffer using the addresses, the protocol and the identification field, and it discards buffers that have waited too long for the missing pieces.

viz.caption: THE FOUR TESTS THE ALGORITHM MAKES ON EACH HOLE

items.title: Fragment starts after the hole
items.text: Test: fragment.first is greater than hole.last. The fragment does not overlap this hole, so the hole is left alone.

items.title: Fragment ends before the hole
items.text: Test: fragment.last is less than hole.first. Again the fragment does not touch this hole.

items.title: Fragment overlaps the hole
items.text: Neither test above is true, so the old hole descriptor is deleted and the hole is described again from whatever is still missing.

items.title: A smaller hole is left
items.text: A new descriptor is created for the part of the hole in front of the fragment, and for the part behind it when the more fragments flag is set.

viz.caption: ILLUSTRATIVE: THE EIGHT STEPS CONDENSED FROM THE RFC

data.title: Fragment processing, condensed
data.code:
1. take the next hole; if there are none, go to 8
2. if fragment.first > hole.last, go to 1
3. if fragment.last < hole.first, go to 1
4. delete the hole descriptor
5. if fragment.first > hole.first, add a hole from hole.first to fragment.first - 1
6. if fragment.last < hole.last and more fragments, add a hole from fragment.last + 1 to hole.last
7. go to 1
8. if the hole list is empty, the datagram is complete
